title: Sharp taste-belief regions with imperfect revelation and bounded preference drift
scope: Sensitivity extension of the source's known-index employer model when information does not fully equalize beliefs and the taste parameter may change across regimes.
significance: Characterizes the exact joint mechanism set and robust sign conditions, quantifying the separate identifying costs of incomplete belief equalization and taste instability.
body:
# Sharp taste-belief regions under imperfect revelation

The source's information-factorial inversion requires equal beliefs after quality revelation and a stable taste cost. Relaxing both assumptions in bounded form yields an exact joint identified set. The resulting uncertainty cannot be inferred from the raw callback contrast without retaining the common index normalization.

Keep interior callback probabilities and the source's known strictly increasing noise distribution \(F\). Let
\[
d_b=F^{-1}(p_{1b})-F^{-1}(p_{0b}),\qquad
d_b=\delta_b-\tau_b,\quad b=0,1.
\]
Here \(\delta_b\) is the cue difference in believed productive value, and \(\tau_b\) is the taste cost in regime \(b\). Replace perfect revelation and taste stability by supplied bounds
\[
|\delta_1|\le\epsilon,\qquad
|\tau_1-\tau_0|\le s,\qquad \epsilon,s\ge0.
\tag{A}
\]
These are restrictions on economic mechanisms in the index units, not estimated facts.

The sharp joint region for the ordinary-regime mechanisms is
\[
\tau_0\in[-d_1-\epsilon-s,\,-d_1+\epsilon+s],
\qquad
\delta_0=d_0+\tau_0.
\tag{B}
\]
Thus the two components lie on a line segment, not in the Cartesian product of their marginal intervals. If the maintained model also requires \(\tau_0\ge0\), intersect the segment with that halfspace. Additional known belief or taste bounds are intersected in the same way; an empty intersection rejects the combined restrictions.

To prove necessity, write \(e=\tau_1-\tau_0\). The informed-regime equation gives
\[
\tau_0=\delta_1-d_1-e.
\]
The difference of independently bounded scalars \(\delta_1\in[-\epsilon,\epsilon]\) and \(e\in[-s,s]\) fills exactly \([-\epsilon-s,\epsilon+s]\), proving the interval. The ordinary equation gives its joint line restriction.

For sufficiency, take any \(\tau_0\) in that interval. Choose \(\delta_1,e\) within their bounds with \(\delta_1-e=\tau_0+d_1\), and set \(\tau_1=\tau_0+e\). Then \(\delta_1-\tau_1=d_1\). Put \(\delta_0=d_0+\tau_0\). For either regime choose the cue-zero belief level as
\[
\mu_{0b}=k+F^{-1}(p_{0b}),
\]
and cue-one level \(\mu_{1b}=\mu_{0b}+\delta_b\). The cue-one index becomes \(F^{-1}(p_{1b})\), so all four observed binary callback distributions are reproduced exactly. No restrictions on belief levels beyond (A) were imposed. This proves sharpness rather than only a triangle-inequality outer bound.

For an illustrative index configuration \(d_0=-0.4,d_1=-0.1\), take \(\epsilon=0.03\), \(s=0.02\). Equation (B) yields
\[
\tau_0\in[0.05,0.15],\qquad
\delta_0\in[-0.35,-0.25].
\]
Both a positive ordinary taste cost and a negative belief difference are robustly present in this model. With \(\epsilon+s\ge0.1\), a zero taste cost becomes compatible with the same callbacks. The data have not changed; the maintained information and stability restrictions have.

At \(\epsilon=s=0\), (B) recovers exactly the manuscript's inversion \(\tau=-d_1,\delta_0=d_0-d_1\). The two uncertainty sources enter additively, but their interpretations remain distinct: imperfect information leaves a belief gap, while regime drift changes preferences.

This is a structural sensitivity region, not an empirical allocation of discriminatory mechanisms. It retains the common threshold and known noise scale, excludes recruitment networks, and does not convert callback evidence into a career earnings effect. Unknown regime-specific noise scales or selective quality validation require a different model.

title: Closed-form sharp mediation bounds using all observed binary cells
scope: Full observed message-belief-compliance cell data under monotone beliefs and monotone baseline compliance, without message exclusion.
significance: Solves the source's 64-type linear-program target analytically in the two-monotonicity subclass: natural mediation lies exactly between zero and min(belief-complier mass, baseline low-belief noncompliance mass).
body:
# Closed-form mediation bounds using all binary cells

The source's response-type linear program is valid and sharp. Under its two optional monotonicities, the full observed binary experiment admits a simple closed-form solution. It is generally tighter than the marginal-response bound when no separate controlled-belief experiment is available.

Assume
\[
B(1)\ge B(0),\qquad C(0,1)\ge C(0,0),
\]
with randomized message assignment and otherwise unrestricted binary response types. Let the observed cells be \(q_z(b,c)\), and set
\[
u=\Pr(B=1\mid Z=1)-\Pr(B=1\mid Z=0),\qquad
r=q_0(0,0).
\]
Provided the data satisfy \(u\ge0\), the exact sharp interval for the source's natural mediated effect is
\[
0\le\tau_B\le\min(u,r).
\tag{A}
\]
No exclusion \(C(z,b)=C(b)\) is imposed. If \(u<0\), monotone beliefs are incompatible with the data.

For necessity, monotonicity partitions the population into always-high, belief-complier and never-high types, with masses
\[
a=\Pr(B=1\mid Z=0),\quad
u,\quad n=\Pr(B=0\mid Z=1).
\]
They sum to one. Natural mediation is positive only for belief compliers whose baseline compliance response changes from zero to one. This event is contained both in the complier group of mass \(u\) and in the observed baseline event \(B(0)=0,C(0,B(0))=0\) of mass \(r\). It has no negative contributions under the two monotonicities. This proves (A).

Here is a construction establishing that every value \(x\in[0,\min(u,r)]\) is attainable while preserving all observed cells. Let \(s=q_0(0,1)\), so \(r+s=n+u\). Choose a mass \(z\) of compliers with baseline compliance zero satisfying
\[
\max(x,u-s,0)\le z\le\min(u,r).
\]
Such a choice exists: \(u-s\le r\) follows from \(r+s=n+u\), and \(u-s\le u\). Allocate \(z\) compliers to baseline zero and \(u-z\) to baseline one. The remaining baseline cells are filled by never-high types, giving their required total mass \(n\).

Among the \(z\) baseline-zero compliers, assign exactly mass \(x\) the response \(C(0,1)=1\), and the remainder zero. For baseline-one compliers, monotone compliance forces \(C(0,1)=1\). Thus the mediated effect is exactly \(x\). For never-high types, set the unobserved \(C(0,1)\) no lower than their baseline response. For always-high types, reproduce the observed baseline \(C(0,1)\) cells and choose unobserved \(C(0,0)=0\). All baseline response restrictions now hold.

Treatment compliance \(C(1,b)\) is unrestricted by these monotonicities. Within the never-high group choose it to reproduce \(q_1(0,c)\). Across the combined always-high and complier group choose it to reproduce \(q_1(1,c)\). Their masses match exactly, and arbitrary correlation with the baseline assignments is permitted. This preserves the complete observed experimental distribution. Fractional masses are valid response-type population probabilities, so the construction also attains both endpoints.

For example, if the message raises high-fairness belief prevalence by \(u=0.4\), but only \(r=0.1\) of the baseline arm jointly have low belief and noncompliance, natural mediation cannot exceed \(0.1\). The remaining belief response cannot generate positive baseline compliance changes for people already compliant. A zero mediated effect still fits, because all message compliance effects may operate through other paths.

The interval is sharp for this complete-cell information class. A separate belief experiment, message exclusion, measurement restrictions or monotonicity of message effects can tighten it further and should be retained jointly. The report does not validate the two monotonicities, treat reported beliefs as error-free in practice, or identify the empirical fairness mechanism.

title: Finite forgiveness restores recurrent clientelism after false alarms
scope: Finite-punishment extension of the source's repeated public-monitoring transfer game with the same timing, signal laws and payoff primitives.
significance: Derives the exact forgiveness threshold and stationary support fraction, showing how a finite strategy sustains recurrent support despite false alarms while preserving secrecy impossibility.
body:
# Finite forgiveness after false monitoring alarms

The source shows that its grim-trigger equilibrium ends almost surely when false alarms occur. A finite-punishment strategy repairs that persistence issue within the same repeated game. Its incentive threshold and long-run support frequency can be derived exactly.

Keep \(d>0,R>0\), discount \(\delta\in(0,1)\), prescribed benefit \(b\le\bar b\), and \(0\le q_1<q_0\le1\). Choose an integer punishment length \(L\ge1\). In the good state the party pays \(b\), the voter supports, and a bad signal starts \(L\) punishment periods at the next date. During punishment the party pays zero and the voter opposes; broker signals are ignored, the counter decreases deterministically, and cooperation resumes afterward. A payment deviation in the good state causes immediate opposition and starts \(L\) punishment periods next date. Nonprescribed payments during punishment do not change the countdown.

Let \(V,P\) be start-of-period good-state voter and party values. Starting a punishment spell has values \(\delta^LV,\delta^LP\), since current punishment payoffs are zero for both sides. Define
\[
D_L=1-\delta+\delta q_1(1-\delta^L)>0.
\]
The good-state Bellman equations give
\[
V=(b-d)/D_L,\qquad P=(R-b)/D_L.
\tag{A}
\]

After receiving \(b\), the voter's support incentive is exactly
\[
d\le\delta(q_0-q_1)(1-\delta^L)V.
\]
Substitution from (A) yields the threshold
\[
b\ge b_L:=
d\left[
\frac{q_0}{q_0-q_1}
+\frac{1-\delta}{\delta(q_0-q_1)(1-\delta^L)}
\right].
\tag{B}
\]
The party's best good-state payment deviation is zero, followed by immediate opposition and delayed return to cooperation. Its deviation value is \(\delta^{L+1}P\). Hence compliance is optimal exactly when \(P\ge0\), or \(b\le R\).

During punishment the voter gains nothing from support because the countdown is action-independent, so opposition is strictly optimal. The party obtains no support from any payment there and optimally pays zero. These one-period conditions therefore hold at every public history; bounded discounted payoffs make the one-deviation principle applicable. The specified finite strategy is sequentially implementable if and only if
\[
b_L\le b\le\min(R,\bar b)
\]
within this strategy class.

The threshold decreases strictly with \(L\), and
\[
\lim_{L\to\infty}b_L
=\frac{d(1-\delta+\delta q_0)}
       {\delta(q_0-q_1)},
\]
the source's grim-trigger threshold. Finite forgiveness sacrifices punishment severity and thus requires a larger benefit. If the resource cap lies strictly above the grim threshold, some finite \(L\) is feasible; if it equals the grim threshold exactly, no finite \(L\) reaches that equality.

When \(q_1>0\), the induced public-state chain has a good spell of expected length \(1/q_1\), followed by exactly \(L\) punishment periods. Its stationary good-state fraction is
\[
\pi_G=\frac1{1+Lq_1}.
\tag{C}
\]
This can also be checked from stationary flows: every punishment state has probability \(q_1\pi_G\), and the \(L+1\) state probabilities sum to one. The finite irreducible chain returns to cooperation infinitely often almost surely. Consequently support has a positive long-run frequency, unlike the source's grim strategy, which eventually ends permanently. If \(q_1=0\), the equilibrium path stays good forever.

Longer punishments lower the required benefit in (B) but lower the stationary support fraction in (C). This gives a precise incentive-versus-false-alarm tradeoff. Perfect secrecy still defeats this monitoring mechanism: at \(q_0=q_1\), a support deviation changes no signal distribution, so no finite benefit paid before voting can compensate its current cost through future sanctions.

This is an additional equilibrium construction, not a characterization of every repeated-game outcome. It retains the source's observable payments, broker technology, no competing party and no reciprocity preference. It neither identifies actual monitoring nor makes transfers themselves a social resource gain.
